title: Roosevelt Island - Manhattan Healing Forest
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded in the Manhattan Healing Forest, our survey station is Roosevelt Island’s Southpoint Park, beginning June 24, 2026. This data was last updated August 13, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Eastern Red Bats and Hoary Bats: NYC’s Migratory Bats of the Summer
Roosevelt Island’s most common species is the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis), which makes up the vast majority of our bat detections at this site (depicted in the graph above in green). This is the most common bat in most of New York City throughout the summer. We also see a very small number of hoary bats (Lasiurus cinereus), an uncommon local species, on Roosevelt Island. If you look close, you can see a golden yellow sliver that starts around August 2nd, this indicates hoary bat numbers have started to pick up with the beginning of August.
Though both of these species live in New York City throughout the summer, they are migratory and will head south as temperatures begin to drop in the fall. The early August increase in hoary bat activity could represent a migratory wave of bats passing through NYC on their way to their wintering destinations.



Eastern Red Bat



Hoary Bat




About iDig2Learn and the Manhattan Healing Forest, our community partners on Roosevelt Island
Our community partner and liaison is Christina Delfico, the local organizing force behind the Manhattan Healing Forest and the founder of the nature-centric organization, iDig2Learn. The Manhattan Healing Forest is New York State’s first Miyawaki Method Pocket Forest. Roughly the size of a tennis court, it contains tight knit plantings of 1,500 native trees and shrubs in Southpoint Park. The pocket forest’s funding partners SUGi, along with leaders from NYS’s Roosevelt Island Operating Corporation (RIOC), the Lenape Center and the Yakama Nation contributed to the community planting of forty-seven native plant species in April 2024. In addition to bats, this small forest corner on Roosevelt Island is also home to kestrels, hawks, falcons, endangered Monarch butterflies and native bees.
“Creating this pocket forest is an invitation to understand how rebuilding soil health positively affects the health of all surrounding life. Using this tight-knit planting Miyawaki Method to strengthen root connections which in turn boosts tree growth exponentially mirrors how diverse communities can come close together now and do this. After all, New Yorkers understand crowded small spaces and if we can plant it here it can plant it anywhere.” -Christina Delfico, founder iDig2Learn



The Manhattan Healing Forest During Planting



2 Years After Planting, photos by Dino Kuznik, courtesy of SUGi

title: McCarren Demonstration Garden at McCarren Park - Williamsburg, BK
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the McCarren Demonstration Garden in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. This garden was the site of a bat rescue earlier this summer and we began monitoring on June 6, 2026. This data was last updated August 4, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Eastern Red Bats: A flexible species
The two most commonly detected species at the McCarren Demonstration Garden are the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis) and big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus). You can see by the alternating colors above that they regularly fluctuate in terms of who is more common.
Red bats are very nomadic, moving their home every one to two days, and flexible in the type of habitat they are willing to use. In the challenging landscape of New York City, this can be a strength. McCarren Park is a great example of this. Though it is far from fresh water and larger, forested parks, red bats are still able to find and take refuge in McCarren Park’s limited habitat. Keep an eye on the baseball lights nearby during the summer and you may even see the occasional red bat feeding off the bugs they attract.



Eastern Red Bat



Big Brown Bat




About McCarren Park Demonstration Garden
We first began working with McCarren Park Demonstration Garden when they invited our principal ecologist, Nic, to give a talk about urban bats in 2025. After a pregnant red bat was discovered hiding in their planting beds earlier this summer, we set up a monitoring station in the garden. From their website:
The McCarren Park Demonstration Garden is an initiative of North Brooklyn Mutual Aid and GrowNYC. We’re a space for environmental education and climate justice, and we’re so happy you’re here.
There are no individual plots in our garden—we grow everything together. We focus on food and flowers to stock our local free fridges. In 2024, we harvested 935 lbs of produce for our neighbors! We also provide free workshops and events for the community, and a chance to make new friends while getting your hands a little dirty.

title: Green-Wood Cemetery, Greenwood Heights, BK
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at Green-Wood Cemetery in central Brooklyn. Surveys this year began on May 10th and this data was last updated August 29, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Not just a cemetery: Green-Wood’s unique value for NYC’s bats
Since first opening the cemetery to our bat surveys in 2024, Green-Wood has become our longest-running research partner and a crucial window into what bat activity can be like in NYC’s green spaces. The first year of surveys revealed the cemetery to host surprisingly high bat activity levels, even matching levels found in rural areas with far more habitat and resources like the Adirondack Mountains of upstate New York. Every year of subsequent research has helped us better understand why bats are so drawn to the cemetery and how unique this area is compared to other parks in the city.
In 2025, we found evidence that the cemetery was uniquely appealing to big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus), hosting, on average, 8x the big brown bat activity of neighboring Prospect Park. Furthermore, this species seemed especially drawn to the resource-rich areas around the park’s border, while the center of the park was dominated by a different bat species, the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis).
Surveys in the cemetery over the winter of 2025/2026 revealed some of the first evidence that our migratory bat species, like hoary bats (Lasiurus cinereus) and silver-haired bats (Lasionycteris noctivagans) may breed in the cemetery during brief winter-time activity bouts.



A “hot spot” map of big brown activity in Green-Wood



Big Brown Bat




Bat Walks at Green-Wood Cemetery
Urban Bat Project NYC is proud to be Green-Wood’s official partner for bat walks. The cemetery hosts several bat walks a year, though they tend to fill up quickly. We recommend keeping a close eye on their summer events calendar for anyone interested. We also host one event our own on the cemetery grounds each year (thanks in large part to the generosity of Green-Wood’s events department). In 2026, Green-Wood was the site of our first combination bat watching and star gazing event.


About Green-Wood Cemetery
Green-Wood Cemetery is one of New York City’s oldest best-known landmarks and one of the oldest examples of a “rural” cemetery in the nation. Beyond its rich history and landmark status, the cemetery is also an incredible supporter of urban ecological research. Each year, they award an environmental fellowship to support research within the cemetery. We are very grateful to have been a recipient of this fellowship in 2025. To learn more about the cemetery, we recommend visiting the official Green-Wood website.

title: Brooklyn Botanic Garden - Crown Heights, BK
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden in Crown Heights, Brooklyn. This is our first year working with BBG and our surveys started on July 16. This data was last updated August 25, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Central Brooklyn: A Tremendous Amount of Bats
Like nearby Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn Botanic Garden (BBG) hosts a surprising amount of bat activity. Note this season’s peak around July 20th when the number of bat detections for a single night neared 900! The garden’s abundant fresh water, open forest, and attachment to larger Prospect Park are all features that make it a bat oasis in the urban landscape of central Brooklyn. Both Prospect Park and Green-Wood Cemetery also sit on an elevated geological feature, known as the Harbor Hill Moraine, and experience slightly higher wind speeds than nearby parts of the landscape. This may make it easier for migratory species like the eastern red bat to navigate in and out of these parks.



The small ponds and loose forest in Brooklyn Botanic Garden, such as the Japanese pond pictured here, create valuable foraging and roosting habitat for bats





The Harbor Hill moraine exists as a large hill running through the center of Brooklyn and Queens today, but it was originally a ridge made of debris from the last ice age




About the Brooklyn Botanic Garden
Founded in 1910, Brooklyn Botanic Garden connects people to the wonder and power of plants, sparking delight and curiosity about science, culture, and our environment to help create a greener, more sustainable city and world. Situated on 52 acres in the heart of Brooklyn and open year-round, the Garden is home to around 10,000 kinds of plants and more than 30 specialty gardens. Learn more at bbg.org.

title: GrowNYC Teaching Garden at Governor’s Island
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the GrowNYC Teaching Garden on Governor’s Island, a small island just south of Manhattan. We began monitoring bat activity on May 13, 2026. This data was last updated August 30, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










A Stop Over for All of our Local Bat Species
While most of our parks within NYC tend to be dominated by our two most common species, you can see on the graph above that Governor’s Island hosts a significant amount of activity from all four: eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis), big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus), silver-haired bat (Lasionycteris noctivagans), and hoary bat (Lasiurus cinereus). This coastal habitat may be especially easy for migrating bats to spot, but for now we can only speculate as to why Governor’s Island hosts such diversity.



Eastern Red Bat



Big Brown Bat


 Hoary Bat


 Silver-haired Bat




About the GrowNYC Teaching Garden on Governor’s Island
As we prepared to wrap up our research season in 2025, we received a message on Instagram about a bat visiting some fig trees on Governor’s Island. Intrigued, we began chatting with the farmer that submitted the observation and GrownNYC’s teaching garden on the island became a top priority site for monitoring this year.



An eastern red bat sleeps in a fig tree on Governor’s Island. Photo by Jules White


Our primary contact on the island is farmer, law student, bird watcher, and bicycling wonder, Jules White. Jules has been an amazing supporter of Urban Bat Project, helping with the Governor’s Island surveys and our winter research in Green-Wood Cemetery. From GrowNYC’s website:
The GrowNYC Teaching Garden on Governors Island is a one-acre urban farm that aims to engage, excite, and educate New Yorkers in all aspects of urban farming and food. We hosts K-12 field trips, public workshops, and donate excess produce we grow to NYC partners from May to October. Discover the power of urban farming, fresh food, and climate action by planning your next visit!



Our local partner, Jules White, in front of the Teaching Garden

title: The High Line Bat Study - Chelsea, Manhattan
text:
The graphs below display bat activity recorded along the High Line in Manhattan this summer. We currently have four bat detectors on the High Line that move every week, an approach that allows us to assess differences in bat activity between different sections of the park. If you compare the two graphs from detectors Pierogi and Knish, you can see that bat activity varies quite a bit along the park.
This data was last updated August 12, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).



















The Flexibility of Eastern Red Bats: A Developing Picture
Over the course of our study we have detected all four of NYC’s common bat species on the High Line, but activity is dominated by the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis). This species is highly tolerant of artificial light, noise, and other aspect of the urban environment that can deter other bats. This likely explains why this species is willing to brave the High Line’s busy surroundings to reach the valuable roosting and foraging habitat the park offers, but we still have much to learn. This research is revealing new information about the eastern red bat and how flexible their habitat preferences really are.



Eastern Red Bat



Red bat activity developing along the High Line this summer




Why are the Detectors named after food?



One of our four High Line detectors


We use a smaller detector on the High Line (pictured above) that features a locking clam-shell case. It naturally invites comparison to any envelope-shaped food, of which there are many to choose from in New York City. In addition to Knish and Pierogi, the High Line is also monitored by our other mini detectors, Ravioli and Dumpling.


Our Partners: the High Line Emerging Leaders Program
The Emerging Leaders Program is a fellowship offered by the High Line to local high school students. It offers early career learning opportunities in public engagement, horticulture, and ecology. The 2026 Emerging Leaders fellow have been a crucial part of collecting the data displayed above. A group meets with our principal ecologist, Nic, every week to keep the detectors working and moving along the park. Special thanks to the “bat captain”, Jiaxiang Zhang.

title: Greenway Botanical Garden at the Naval Cemetery Landscape - Williamsburg, BK
text:
The graph below displays bat activity recorded at the Botanical Garden at Naval Cemetery Landscape in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. This is our second year working with the Brooklyn Greenway Initiative at this site, with this year’s surveys beginning on May 29, 2026. This data was last updated August 15, 2026. The graph displays the survey nights in chronological order from left to right (x-axis) and and the number of bats detected each night are represented by the vertical peaks and valleys (y-axis).










Big Brown Bats and Eastern Red Bats: Two Very Different Approaches to NYC
The two most commonly detected species at the Naval Cemetery Landscape are the eastern red bat (Lasiurus borealis) and big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus). You can see by the alternating colors above that they regularly fluctuate in terms of who is more common.
Eastern red bats are nomadic, migratory bats that spend the summer in NYC. They typically move to a new location every 1-2 days and are extremely flexible in their habitat requirements. Big brown bats, on the other hand, are very particular about finding the best quality habitat available. Once they’ve found a spot they like, they’ll make it their home until its time for them to hibernate in the winter.



Eastern Red Bat



Big Brown Bat




About the Brooklyn Greenway Initiative and the Botanical Garden at Naval Cemetery Landscape
Brooklyn Greenway Initiative is the team behind the restoration of Naval Cemetery Landscape. We began working with them in 2025 and they have been incredible partners in research. In 2026, we began offering bat walks at this location. From their website:
Brooklyn Greenway Initiative built the Naval Cemetery Landscape (now called the Greenway Botanical Garden at the Naval Cemetery) in 2016 on the site of the former Naval Hospital Cemetery at the Brooklyn Navy Yard as a place for retreat and remembrance while honoring its rich layers of natural and cultural history. This site was designed as a native plant meadow and pollinator habitat, and provides visitors with an escape from urban life. Many rare birds and insects can be seen here. There are magnifying glasses on site and visitors are encouraged to bring their own binoculars to observe the bird species from the boardwalk
